reasoning.notes: In the original hands players read voids from discards, counted the trumps and suit cards still out, and fed points onto tricks their partner was sure to win. In the replays nearly every decision rests on an exact, correct rebuild of all four hands, and score arithmetic is used to decide whether points or control matter more.

evidence.quote: has my old hand 1 cards: DQ, S5, CK, HQ, SQ, HA. It holds hearts, so it must follow the heart lead and cannot trump.
evidence.shows: Correct inference of an opponent's exact hand from the replay structure, used to find a cheap winning trump.

evidence.quote: The only heart I can't account for is H5, so seat 4 is probably out of hearts and may trump.
evidence.shows: Card counting to infer a likely void during a hidden-information hand.

evidence.quote: Team A stays at 225 and 60 points are left. Our best possible total is 225, so a draw is still possible.
evidence.shows: Exact match-score arithmetic used to pick the only card that keeps a draw possible.

planning.notes: Players repeatedly made plans spanning several tricks and carried them out. These plans strip opponents' trumps while saving a sole top trump for the doubled-kitty 6th trick, and several rely on forced plays by opponents and partner. Examples are the C5 lead in match 1 hand 3, the joker sequence in match 3 hand 3, and the H5-then-keep-HK plan in match 1 hand 4.

evidence.quote: Seat 4 must follow with CK. Seat 1 wins with CA... Seat 1 then leads DA... Seat 1 next leads H5. Seat 2 is out of hearts, and I win the trick with SA.
evidence.shows: A three-trick plan built on the forced plays of both opponents and partner; it was carried out.

evidence.quote: If I lead H5, seat 2 must play the Big Joker... If I keep HK as my last card, it is legal on trick 6 whatever suit is led, and it wins.
evidence.shows: Spending a low trump to force out the opponent's top trump, keeping a sure winner for the doubled kitty.

evidence.quote: If I lead both jokers first, seat 4 must follow with a trump each time. That uses up both SA and S10... My SK then wins the last trick
evidence.shows: A trump-drawing sequence planned over the rest of the hand and executed exactly.

luck.notes: The duplicate replay cancels deal luck, and in the replays everyone has full information, so outcomes were mostly decided by play. Chance mattered only at the margins of the original hands, such as unseen voids or where the kitty sat.

evidence.quote: With that many out, each opponent probably still holds a club and must follow suit, so my ace is less likely to be trumped.
evidence.shows: A sound probabilistic lead that failed because seat 2 happened to be void (trumped with H5); hidden distribution moved a few points.

weak_spots.what: Seat 4 knew from the replay that seat 1 held both jokers and no hearts, so any heart lead would be trumped. It still led H10, giving away 10 points. Leading HQ would have lost the trick for 10 fewer points.
Seat 1 spent the Big Joker to take a 10-point trick, giving up control of the last trick. Seat 2's HK then won the 30-point 6th trick, so keeping the Joker for the finish was likely better.
Seat 4 led SK while SA was unaccounted for, and it lost 15 points to seat 3's SA. Leading a joker first would have drawn out the outstanding trumps without exposing the King.

summary: Winning takes real reasoning and planning: counting and void inference in the original hands, and multi-trick trump-stripping plans aimed at the doubled-kitty 6th trick, especially in the replays. Because the replays give everyone full information, the game would demand more inference if the replays were not announced, or if the hand passed on were partly hidden, so hidden-hand reasoning stayed central throughout.
